lines: Nine tables. The same data, joined the same way, asking for the same count.
One version of that question reports a total cost. Another version reports a much smaller one.
Nothing about the tables changed between them. So what did?
A table's page count and row count are sitting right there in the catalog, along with the two constants the planner uses to turn them into a cost.
Work the arithmetic by hand before the planner shows its own number.
Does the planner's reported cost land on the smaller figure, the larger one, or something else entirely?
answer: It lands on the sum of the two pieces: the page count times the sequential page cost, plus the row count times the per row cost.
That is the whole formula, worked by hand on a real table instead of a toy one.

lines: Here is the planner's own reported number, printed right where the hand arithmetic predicted it would be.
Not an estimate rounded for convenience. An exact match, to the decimal.
A plan's cost is never measured after the query runs. It is computed, in the planner's own arbitrary units, before a single row moves.
Five numbers do all the work: one for a sequential page, a larger one for a page fetched out of order, and three small ones for the cost of touching each row, each index entry, and each operator.
Every plan the planner ever considers is priced from just these five.
Whichever plan's total comes out lowest is the one that runs.
Scanning one table barely counts as a decision. Choosing the order to join many tables is a different kind of problem.
Count every distinct way to join twelve tables and the number runs past twenty eight trillion. Push to fourteen tables and it is past sixty four quadrillion.
That count was not guessed at. It was checked by brute force on small cases before it was trusted on large ones.
The sheer size of that search is the actual reason a planner needs a strategy at all, not just a cost formula.
Nine tables, written in the worst possible order. The one selective filter sits last, after eight unfiltered joins have already run.
A setting limits how many tables the planner is allowed to freely reorder, and by default that limit is smaller than nine.
Will the planner still find its way to a better order, or is it stuck with the order as written?
answer: Stuck with it. Nine tables is one more than the default limit covers, so the planner cannot flatten and freely reorder the whole list.
The order on the page is the order that actually runs.

lines: Force the planner to keep that literal, bad order and the total cost is enormous — every unfiltered table joined in full before the one real filter ever applies.
Let the planner reorder freely instead, and the total cost drops to a small fraction of that — more than ten times smaller.
Same tables. Same data. Same question being asked. The only thing that changed was whether the planner was allowed to rewrite what was written.
Two settings, both defaulting to the same modest number, control this: one for how many tables a written join can flatten into, one for how many a merged subquery can.
Pin that number down to its smallest possible value and you are telling the planner: keep the order exactly as I wrote it.
That is not a workaround for a bug. It is the deliberate way to force a join order you already know is better.
There is a threshold, measured in how many tables a query touches at once, past which the planner changes its whole strategy.
Push a chain of joins from just under that threshold to just over it.
Does the plan get better past that point, worse, or does nothing change at all?
answer: Worse is possible, but faster to find is the actual trade. Past the threshold the planner swaps an exhaustive search for a much quicker, less certain one.
It gives up a guarantee of finding the best order in exchange for a bound on how long finding any order takes.

lines: Force the exhaustive search anyway, past that threshold, and watch planning time itself: a small fraction of a second at eight tables, well over a second at twelve, dozens of seconds at fourteen.
Push two tables further still and the exhaustive search never returned an answer at all — the attempt alone was enough to strain the whole server.
Switch to the quicker strategy at those same sizes and planning finishes in a small fraction of a second, landing on exactly the same cost both times, here.
A bound on how long the search takes, not a promise about what the search finds — this particular query just happened to get both anyway.
That quicker strategy treats a join order the way an old routing puzzle treats a tour between cities: encode the order as a string of stops, and let a whole population of candidate strings compete.
Cheaper candidates survive. The most expensive ones are discarded, and new candidates are bred by recombining pieces of the ones that survived.
A genuine search through a sample of the space, not a shortcut through the whole thing.
One more thing the planner tracks that has nothing to do with cost alone: the order rows already come out in.
Ask for rows in a particular order with no help from an index and the planner adds an explicit sorting step, at real cost.
Add an index that already produces rows in that exact order and the sorting step disappears entirely. The total cost drops by more than a thousand times.
A scan is not just priced on how it reads rows — it is also valued for the order it happens to leave them in.
Before trusting any plan's shape, three questions are worth asking.
What do those five constants assume about the hardware underneath — is a random read on this machine really that much slower than a sequential one?
Would a smaller reorder limit have blocked the planner from reaching a better order here?
And is this query already past the point where the quicker, less certain search took over?
A smaller table this time: a couple thousand pages, tens of thousands of rows.
Using the same five constants as before, what total cost does a sequential scan of it report?
answer: The same formula as before, just smaller numbers going in: the page count times the sequential page cost, plus the row count times the per row cost.
Once the formula is in hand, any table's number is just arithmetic.

lines: Seven tables this time, also written in a bad order, with the reorder limit left at its ordinary default.
Does seven fit comfortably under that default, or does it run into the same wall nine did?
answer: It fits. Seven is within the default limit, so the planner can still flatten the whole list and search freely, no matter how it was written.
The wall only shows up once the written join actually exceeds the limit — which is exactly what made nine tables different from seven.
